prompt: What does a checkpoint do?
hint: After one, the dirty count was 0 and grep found the row in the table's file.

choices.text: Copies the data directory to a backup
choices.why: Nothing is copied anywhere. Backups belong to db-reliability.

choices.text: Writes every dirty page to its file and records where recovery would start
choices.why: Right. After it, the log written before its redo point is no longer needed.

choices.text: Commits every transaction still open, so that none of them is lost in a crash
choices.why: A checkpoint never decides a transaction's fate; open transactions stay open.

choices.text: Flushes the WAL buffers, which COMMIT leaves in memory
choices.why: COMMIT flushes its own log records before returning. A checkpoint is about table pages.

prompt: `pg_controldata` shows a REDO location that is earlier than the checkpoint location. Why are they different?
hint: The log keeps growing while the pages are written.

choices.text: The checkpoint starts at one and writes its record at the other
choices.why: Right. Changes made while pages were written are covered by replaying from the start point.

choices.text: The REDO location belongs to the previous checkpoint
choices.why: Both lines describe the latest checkpoint: the first is where it started, the second where it ended.

choices.text: One is in the log, the other in the table files
choices.why: Both are positions in the log. Table files have no LSN of their own in pg_control.

choices.text: A replica moved the REDO location back
choices.why: This server had no replica; the gap is how every checkpoint works.

prompt: Match each part of a `checkpoint complete` line to what it reports.
hint: One is pages, one is segments, one is log, one is the disk.

pairs.right: dirty pages written to their files
log written since the previous checkpoint
time waiting for the disk to confirm

prompt: Right after the `CHECKPOINT` command, the dirty count in `pg_buffercache` was 0. A minute later on a busy server it is 3000. What does that mean?
hint: Commits keep changing pages in memory.

choices.text: 3000 pages changed since then
choices.why: Right. Each is safe in the log and waits for the next checkpoint or the background writer.

choices.text: The checkpoint failed
choices.why: It reported checkpoint complete and the count did reach 0. New changes came after it.

choices.text: Those 3000 commits are at risk until the next checkpoint
choices.why: Their log records reached the disk at COMMIT. Dirty pages are rebuilt from the log after a crash.

choices.text: shared_buffers is too small and must be raised
choices.why: Dirty pages are normal work, not a sign of memory pressure.

prompt: The log shows `checkpoint starting: wal`. What started that checkpoint?
hint: The other routine kind says time.

choices.text: checkpoint_timeout running out
choices.why: That one is logged as time.

choices.text: Somebody typing CHECKPOINT
choices.why: The command is logged as immediate force wait.

choices.text: The walwriter filling the WAL buffers
choices.why: The walwriter flushes buffers; it never starts a checkpoint.

choices.text: Enough log written since the last one
choices.why: Right. A little under half of max_wal_size, by the server's arithmetic.

prompt: With `max_wal_size` at 64MB, how many checkpoints did `pg_stat_bgwriter` count as `checkpoints_req` during the 40,000-transaction run?
hint: None of them were timed.

prompt: With `max_wal_size = 1GB` and the default completion target, roughly how much log is written between two checkpoints forced by WAL?
hint: At 64MB the distance was 32780 kB.

choices.text: Around 500 MB
choices.why: Right. A little under half, as 32 MB was for 64 MB.

choices.text: 1 GB, the setting itself
choices.why: The whole cycle has to fit in max_wal_size, so the trigger comes earlier.

choices.text: 80 MB, the min_wal_size
choices.why: min_wal_size is the floor kept for recycling, not a trigger.

choices.text: 16 MB, one segment per checkpoint
choices.why: A segment is the unit of the files, not of the checkpoint interval.

prompt: A server's log carries `checkpoints are occurring too frequently` every few minutes during the nightly import, and never by day. What is the fitting change?
hint: The HINT names it; think about what it costs.

choices.text: Raise checkpoint_warning so the message stops
choices.why: That silences the alarm and leaves the extra WAL and page images in place.

choices.text: Raise max_wal_size, with disk room for it
choices.why: Right. Fewer forced checkpoints during the import, paid for in pg_wal space and recovery time.

choices.text: Lower checkpoint_timeout to spread the load
choices.why: More timed checkpoints add to the problem; these are already forced by the log.

choices.text: Turn log_checkpoints off during the import
choices.why: The checkpoints still happen; you would only stop seeing them.

prompt: The same 40,000 transactions wrote 461 MB of WAL with 14 checkpoints and 224 MB with none. Where did most of the difference come from?
hint: Compare wal_records and wal_fpi.

choices.text: The checkpoint records themselves
choices.why: Fourteen small records are nothing beside 237 MB.

choices.text: More transactions committed in the first run, which the checkpoints sped up
choices.why: Both ran exactly 40,000: -t 10000 for each of four clients.

choices.text: Full-page images, taken again after each checkpoint
choices.why: Right. Records barely moved; images more than doubled, 59334 against 27489.

choices.text: The dirty pages the checkpoints wrote into the log
choices.why: Checkpoints write pages to the table files, not into the log.

prompt: A colleague wants `full_page_writes = off` on an ext4 server to halve its WAL. What is the argument against?
hint: What repairs a page torn by a power cut?

choices.text: A torn page would be left corrupt, with nothing to repair it
choices.why: Right. Recovery would apply small records onto a half-written page, and nothing would report it.

choices.text: Replicas stop working without the images
choices.why: Replicas replay records either way; the danger is to the primary's own pages after a power cut.

choices.text: The server refuses to start with it off
choices.why: It starts happily, which is the danger: nothing complains until a torn page is read.

choices.text: It saves nothing, because the images are compressed
choices.why: wal_compression is off by default, and the images were most of the extra volume.

prompt: The run at the default `max_wal_size` still took 27489 page images with no checkpoint during it. Why any at all?
hint: What ran just before it?

choices.text: Every update records an image regardless of checkpoints
choices.why: Then the images would equal the updates; 27489 is far below the row changes made.

choices.text: The background writer adds images as it writes pages
choices.why: Images ride with a page's first change, not with writing the page out.

choices.text: It began right after a CHECKPOINT
choices.why: Right. Every page it touched was changed for the first time since that checkpoint, once.

choices.text: pgbench forces a full-page write at the end of each transaction
choices.why: pgbench only sends SQL; it has no say in what the log records.

prompt: After a crash of the server process, what is the first thing to do?
hint: The lesson's server repaired itself.

choices.text: Restore last night's backup
choices.why: That throws away every commit since the backup, which recovery would have kept.

choices.text: Run pg_resetwal so it starts cleanly
choices.why: That discards the log recovery needs, which is how a recoverable server becomes a corrupt one.

choices.text: Start it again, and read what its log says
choices.why: Right. Recovery replays from the redo point by itself and says so line by line.

choices.text: Delete postmaster.pid and the oldest segments in pg_wal
choices.why: Nothing needed deleting; the segments are the material recovery replays.

prompt: Recovery logged `invalid record length at 0/535AA2E0: expected at least 24, got 0`. What does that line mean?
hint: It is a LOG line, and every recovery ends with one like it.

choices.text: A segment is corrupt and data was lost
choices.why: The count of acks matched the client's list exactly. Nothing was lost.

choices.text: Recovery reached the end of the log
choices.why: Right. The next bytes were zeros, never written, so replay stopped there.

choices.text: A record was too short and was skipped
choices.why: Recovery never skips a record and carries on; it stops at the first one that is not valid.

choices.text: The kill interrupted pg_waldump
choices.why: pg_waldump was not running; this is the server reading its own log at start-up.

prompt: After the crash, the client's `acked.txt` ends at 13003. Which result of `SELECT max(id), count(*) FROM acks` would show a broken guarantee?
hint: A commit can reach the disk before its reply reaches the client.

choices.why: Right. A commit the client was told about is missing, which a correctly configured server never does.
That is what the lesson got: every confirmed commit present.
One more is fine: that commit reached the disk and its reply died with the server.

prompt: Put the lines a start-up after a crash writes in order.
hint: It notices, replays, finds the end, checkpoints, opens.
items: database system was not properly shut down; automatic recovery in progress
invalid record length at 0/535AA2E0: expected at least 24, got 0
database system is ready to accept connections
trap: Connections are accepted only after the end-of-recovery checkpoint, not as soon as replay ends.

prompt: With `synchronous_commit = off`, what does a crash lose?
hint: The walwriter flushes every wal_writer_delay.

choices.text: Nothing, because the walwriter flushes before the crash
choices.why: A crash does not wait for the walwriter's next wake-up.

choices.text: The last fraction of a second of commits
choices.why: Right. Those transactions are absent as a whole; the database stays consistent.

choices.text: Every change since the last checkpoint
choices.why: Everything flushed to the log survives; only the unflushed tail goes.

choices.text: Random pages, leaving the tables corrupt
choices.why: That is fsync = off. The write-ahead order still holds with synchronous_commit off.

prompt: Why did the lesson not demonstrate `fsync = off` corrupting the database with `kill -9`?
hint: What survives a kill of the server's processes?

choices.text: kill -9 is refused while fsync is off
choices.why: The kernel delivers SIGKILL whatever the server's settings.

choices.text: fsync = off needs a restart, and the lab could not restart
choices.why: The server restarted in the crash section. The obstacle is what a kill leaves behind.

choices.text: PostgreSQL 16 ignores fsync = off
choices.why: It obeys it, which is exactly the danger.

choices.text: The operating system's cache survives the kill and is written out later
choices.why: Right. Only a power cut or a kernel crash loses that cache, which is why fsync = off passes ordinary tests.

prompt: To skip the wait for the disk in one transaction only, write `SET ___ synchronous_commit = off;` after BEGIN.
hint: It lasts until the end of the transaction.

prompt: The lesson measured about twice the throughput with `synchronous_commit = off`. On a server whose disk takes ten times longer to confirm a flush, what would you expect?
hint: What does a commit wait for when the setting is on?

choices.text: A wider gap
choices.why: Right. With the setting on, each commit waits for that slow flush; off, it does not wait at all.

choices.text: The same ratio, since the setting does the same thing
choices.why: The ratio is set by the cost of the wait the setting removes, and that cost grew.

choices.text: A smaller gap, because slow disks gain less
choices.why: It runs the other way: the slower the flush, the more there is to save by not waiting for it.

choices.text: No difference, because pgbench is limited by the processors
choices.why: The lesson's run already showed the flush mattered, by halving latency.

prompt: Match each setting, when turned off, to what a crash can cost.
hint: One loses a moment, one loses the guarantee, one loses a repair.

pairs.right: the last fraction of a second of acknowledged commits
anything, since nothing orders writes to disk
a page torn by a power cut stays corrupt

prompt: An application inserts page-view events and also records payments. Throughput on the events is the problem. Which change keeps every guarantee the payments need?
hint: A setting can be made for one transaction.

choices.text: ALTER SYSTEM SET synchronous_commit = off
choices.why: That weakens every commit on the server, the payments' included.

choices.text: fsync = off during business hours
choices.why: That risks corrupting the whole database, payments included, on a power cut.

choices.text: full_page_writes = off, but only for the table that holds the events
choices.why: It is not a per-table setting, and it removes the torn-page repair everywhere.

choices.text: SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off in the event transactions
choices.why: Right. The events trade a moment of loss for speed; payments still wait for the disk.

prompt: Raising `max_wal_size` from 1GB to 16GB on a busy server makes which of these worse?
hint: Fewer checkpoints, more log between them.

choices.text: The volume of full-page images written to the log each hour
choices.why: Fewer checkpoints mean fewer images; this improves.

choices.text: The time recovery takes after a crash
choices.why: Right. More log since the last checkpoint means more to replay.

choices.text: How often checkpoints_req climbs
choices.why: Forced checkpoints become rarer, not more frequent.

choices.text: How long each COMMIT waits
choices.why: COMMIT waits for its own log flush, which max_wal_size does not change.

prompt: On Ubuntu, the program that prints pg_control, including the latest checkpoint's REDO location, is /usr/lib/postgresql/16/bin/___.
hint: The file's name, then data.

prompt: A server crashed at 10:00. Its last checkpoint completed at 09:58, and the one before at 09:53. From which point does recovery replay?
hint: pg_control names the latest checkpoint record; that record names a position.

choices.text: The record of the 09:58 checkpoint
choices.why: Changes made while that checkpoint wrote pages lie before its record, so replay starts earlier.

choices.text: The redo point of the 09:58 checkpoint
choices.why: Right. Where that checkpoint started; everything before it is already in the table files.

choices.text: The redo point of the 09:53 checkpoint
choices.why: Only the latest checkpoint matters once it has completed.

choices.text: The oldest segment file that is still present in pg_wal
choices.why: Old segments may still sit there, recycled; recovery goes by the redo point, not by the files present.
